USEFUL PHRASES

body.subtitle: WITH INDEX-VOCABULARY AND OTHER HELPS
body.p: BREWER AND CO., LTD., AND MAX NÖSSLER AND CO.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The compilation of these phrases was suggested by the frequent requests on the part of busy residents or transient visitors for a handbook containing easily-learned every-day words and phrases. The compiler is well aware that there is no royal road or short cut to learning, and would recommend to those who have the time for the more thorough study of the colloquial a careful study of Dr. Hawks Pott’s “Lessons in the Shanghai Dialect” (or Dr. Yates’ First Lessons in Chinese), and a constant use of the Shanghai Vocabulary, as well as the excellent Chinese-English Dictionary prepared by Messrs. Silsby and Davis.

We trust that these phrases will not only be of immediate use to the busy house-wife and merchant, or inquiring tourist, but will be of effective assistance to the student in the acquisition of a knowledge of the idiom. The Chinese mode of thought and method of speech differs so largely from our own that the acquirement of a fluent and familiar use of colloquial Chinese seems only possible by committing to memory, or carefully studying, such sentences as are collected in the following pages. A useful practice would be to rewrite the English word by word, according to the order in the vernacular, so as to perceive the construction of sentences and the peculiar use of verbs, adverbs, prepositions, connective and terminal particles, etc. To aid in the recognition of the English equivalents of the Chinese character or romanised we have added an index and vocabulary of the words used in this book. This will require to be used cautiously, as the meanings given in many cases are not the primary ones, but rather those used in certain phrases. It ought also to be mentioned that the grammatical and topical groups at the end of the book are not complete, but are added for convenience of reference and in the hope that they will tempt to a fuller study through the medium of the more elaborate works.

The description of the romanised system used is reproduced, by kind permission, from the material supplied by Rev. J. A. Silsby to accompany the romanised translation of the Police Regulations published by the Shanghai Municipal Council. This system of romanisation was adopted by the Shanghai Vernacular Society in 1899, and has many merits, not the least being the absence of diacritical marks.

Grateful thanks are accorded to friends who have helped with advice, particularly to Rev. G. F. Fitch, D.D., Rev. J. A. Silsby, and Mr. Kau Voong-dz (高鳳池). Such help was very necessary from the manner in which various native teachers differed as to pronunciation and idiom.

In spite of all the pains taken in the preparation of these sentences and in the revision for this second edition it is possible that errors still remain; the compiler, therefore, will be grateful for corrections, which will be duly noted in prospect of a possible future edition.

div.head: Useful Phrases in the Shanghai Dialect
Description of the Shanghai Romanised System.
div.p: Nearly all the syllables are represented by the combination of an initial and a final, a system which has been found to be well adapted to the Chinese language.

div.head: Initials.
div.p: The Upper Series are—p, ’m, ’v, t, ts, s, ’l, ’ny, ’ng, k, ky, kw, i and ’w. These initials are pronounced in most cases much the same as in English, but without aspiration, higher in pitch and with very little vibration of the larynx. The apostrophe before a letter indicates that the letter belongs to the “higher series.” Pure vowel initials also belong to this series.
’ny has a sound similar to that of ni in spaniel.
ky ＝ ch in chuk with all aspiration eliminated.
i as an initial has the sound of i in dahlia.
The Aspirates are—ph, f, th, tsh, kh, ch, khw, h, hy, and hw (th as in Thomson—not as in thing).
hy is nearly like ti in Portia.
The other aspirates are like the corresponding initials of the higher series with the addition of a strong aspiration (indicated by h).

The Lower Series are—b, m, v, d, dz, z, l, n, ny, ng, g, j, gw, y, and w. Their pronunciation is much the same as in English. They are lower in pitch than corresponding initials of the “higher series,” and have more “voice,” being pronounced with more decided vibration of the larynx. The lower vowel initials, indicated by an inverted comma (‘) and attended with a slight aspiration, belong to this series.

div.head: Finals.
div.p: 1. The Vowel Endings are—a, e, i, au, o, oo, oe, eu, u, ui, ia, iau, ieu, and ie.

2. The Nasal Endings are—(a) an, en, ien and oen, in which the n is not sounded, but lengthens out and imparts a nasal quality to the preceding vowel; (b) ang, aung, oong, (or ong), ung and iang, in which ng has the value of ng in song, but is often nearer the French n in bon; (c) uin, in which n is sonant and has a value varying between n and ng.
3. The Abrupt Vowel Endings are—ak, ah, eh, ih, auh, ok, oeh, uh, and iak, in which h and k are the signs of the zeh-sung (入聲), and the vowel is pronounced in a short, abrupt manner.
The sounds of the vowels are—
a as in far, except when followed by n or h, when it has the sound of a in man or mat.
e as in prey; before h it has the sound of e as in met.
i „ caprice; before h or ng it is shortened to i as in mit or sing.
o or oo as ou in though or in through. It is really a combination of these two sounds, and is modified by its environment.
u „ oo in foot (always preceded by an s sound).
ui „ in fruit (or rather French ü).
In ia, iau, ieu and ie, we have short i followed closely by a, au, eu, and e, as described above.
Of course it is understood that the Chinese sounds in a majority of cases vary somewhat from the English sounds which are given as the nearest equivalent.

The Dok-yoong Z-moo— “Initials used alone” i.e., without vowels, are—ts, tsh, dz, s, z, an, ng, and r. The first five are followed by the vowel sound in the second syllable of able—prolonged. Mateer and Bailer use ï for this sound and the new Mandarin Romanized uses i[C0]. It is not written, but understood in the Shanghai system. m has the sound of m in chasm and ng the sound of ng in hanger; r is a sound between final r and l.
Tone Marks.—As in Ningpo and other Woo dialects, tone marks are unnecessary in ordinary letter-press, and are omitted in this book.

l.hi: Noong iau tsheh-chi, sien kau-soo ngoo.

lg.l: At the end of the month you can go.
做到月底儂可以停 (or 可以去)
Tsoo tau nyoeh-ti, noong khau-i ding (or khau-i chi).
If you go home, you must get me a substitute.
若是儂歸去, 要呌替工

l.hi: Zak-z noong kyiu-chi, iau kyau thi-koong.

lg.l: Can you get me a coolie?
儂可以尋 (or 呌) 一个苦力否
Noong khau-i zing (or kyau) ih-kuh khoo-lih va?
If you want to go (stop work) you must wait till the end of the month.
若是儂要停, 要做到月底

l.hi: Zak-z noong iau ding, iau tsoo tau nyoeh-ti.

lg.l: [If] you want to go (or stop work), you must wait till I find new man.
儂要停, 等我尋著新个人

l.hi: Noong iau ding, tung ngoo zing-dzak sing-kuh nyung.

lg.l: If you go now it is not convenient to pay your wages.
現在停, 勿便付儂工錢

l.hi: Yien-dze ding, ’veh bien foo noong koong-dien.

lg.l: [I] will pay at the end of the month.
[If you] go now I will cut your wages.
現在停, 我要齾儂工錢

l.hi: Yien-dze ding, ngoo iau ngah noong koong-dien.

lg.l: This cook is not a very good one.
This coolie is also very lazy.
I want to put up the stove for this room at once.
Brush these clothes and hang in the sun.
衣裳刷之咾晒拉日頭裡

l.hi: I-zaung seh-ts lau so la nyih-deu li.

lg.l: Be careful the wind does not blow them away.
Take this out and shake it [clean].
Use a rope to tie this.
Buy a basket (with string net on top).
Put all the food into this basket.
吃个物事全擺拉第隻籃裡

l.hi: Chuh-kuh meh-z zen pa-la di-tsak lan-li.

lg.l: Buy me a foot-stove and some charcoal (balls).
買一隻脚爐咾幾个炭團

l.hi: Ma ih-tsak kyak-loo lau kyi-kuh than-doen.

lg.l: Go to the Chinese Imperial Post Office.
Go to the Post Office for the mail.

l.hi: Tau su-sing-kwen chi tan sing le.

lg.l: Take this parcel to the Post Office.

l.hi: Di-kuh pau, soong tau su-sing-kwen chi.

lg.l: Call a wheelbarrow and take these things to the steamer.
呌小車送第个物事到船上去

l.hi: Kyau siau-tsho soong di-kuh meh-z tau zen laung chi.

lg.l: The answer says there are two books; why is there only one here?
回信話有兩本書, 現在只有一本, 啥緣故

l.hi: We-sing wo yeu liang-pung su; yien-dze tsuh-yeu ih-pung, sa yoen-koo?

lg.l: The chit book says there is an answer; where is it?
送信簿上寫明有回信, 拉那裡

l.hi: Soong-sing-boo laung sia-ming yeu we-sing, la ‘a-li?

lg.l: This letter is not mine; have you any other?
第封信勿是我个, 還有別个否

l.hi: Di-fong sing ’veh-z ngoo-kuh; wan yeu bih-kuh va?

lg.l: This is for the next house.
第个物事是隔壁人家个.
Call a man to put a new cover on this chair.
第隻椅子呌人來換新个裿布

l.hi: Di-tsak iui-ts, kyau nyung le wen sing-kuh iui poo.

lg.l: Get a new glass for this broken window.
窗上个碎玻璃要配新个

l.hi: Tshaung-laung-kuh se poo-li iau phe sing-kuh.

lg.l: Take this pass-book to the store and bring the things.
担第本簿子到店裏去, 拿物事來

l.hi: Tan di-pung boo-ts tau tien-li chi, nau meh-z le.

lg.l: Go and buy some bread tickets.
Take these tickets and exchange for bread.

l.hi: Tan di-kuh phiau-ts chi wen men-deu.

lg.l: I want a ricksha to go to the French Concession.
要一部東洋車到法租界去

l.hi: Iau ih-boo toong-yang-tsho tau Fah-tsoo-ka chi.

lg.l: I want a carriage for half a day.

l.hi: Ngoo iau ih-boo mo-tsho yoong pen-nyih.

lg.l: This carriage is not good; get another.
第部馬車勿好, 要換好个
I am not very well to-day (or am ill).
今朝我勿大爽快 (or 有毛病)
Kyung-tsau ngoo ’veh da saung-khwa (or yeu mau-bing).
I don’t know what it is.
I’ll give you a dose of medicine.
You had better see the doctor.
I must go to the hospital.
我要歸去 or 到屋裡去
Ngoo iau kyui-chi (or tau ok-li chi).
You can return home for a short time.
You are still not fit for work.

l.hi: Noong yien-dze wan ’veh nung tsoo sang-weh.

lg.l: Come again when you are stronger.
Cook is sick and can’t get up.
大司務拉生病, 勿能起來
Why do you work so very slowly?
Perhaps you go out too much at night.

l.hi: Khoong-pho noong ya-deu tsheh-chi thuh too.

lg.l: I think you smoke opium (or drink wine.)
我想儂吃雅片煙 (or 吃酒)
Ngoo siang noong chuh ia-phien-ien (or chuh tsieu).
Your clothes and hat are untidy.
Don’t have your shoes down at the heel.
Have you not combed your hair to-day?
If it is too cold, come home.
This you can give to the washerman.
第个可以撥汏衣裳个人淨

l.hi: Di-kuh khau-i peh da-i-zaung-kuh nyung zing.

lg.l: Use hot water to wash flannel.
Hang them up (as on a line to dry or air).
Shake well and hang up in the sun.

l.hi: Iau teu-teu lau so la nyih-deu-li.

lg.l: [When] ironing clothes, do not have them too dry.
衣裳要燙, 勿要忒乾

l.hi: I-zaung iau thaung, ’veh iau thuh koen.

lg.l: I want you to sew this.
我要儂做 (or 縫) 第个
Ngoo iau noong tsoo (or voong) di-kuh.
My children are not very small; so, therefore, I want you to sew and knit and help me (lit., help in hand work).
我个小囝勿算頂小, 所以要儂相帮我做手裡生活

l.hi: Ngoo-kuh siau-noen ’veh soen ting siau, soo-i iau noong siang-paung ngoo tsoo seu-li sang-weh.

lg.l: Put on (baby’s) outdoor clothes and take him out.
著之外罩衣裳咾領伊到外頭去

l.hi: Tsak-ts nga-tsau-i-zaung lau ling yi tau nga-deu chi.

lg.l: Don’t buy anything and give her to eat.

l.hi: ’Veh iau ma sa meh-z peh yi chuh.

lg.l: Don’t give him anything to eat unless I say so.
若是我勿告訴儂末, 儂勿要撥啥伊吃

l.hi: Zak-z ngoo ’veh kau-soo noong meh, noong ’veh iau peh sa yi chuh.

lg.l: Because she is sick she cannot eat this.
爲之伊有毛病, 所以勿能吃第个

l.hi: We-ts yi yeu mau-bing, soo-i ’veh nung chuh di-kuh.

lg.l: My wages are too small, please increase them.
我个工錢勿彀, 請儂加點

l.hi: Ngoo-kuh koong-dien ’veh keu, tshing noong ka-tien.

lg.l: Just now I cannot increase; afterwards I will give you more.
現在我勿能加, 後首咾加儂

l.hi: Yien-dze ngoo ’veh nung ka, ‘eu-seu lau ka noong.

lg.l: If you cannot give more now, I must leave you.
若是儂現在勿能加, 我只得停 (or 離開儂)
Zah-z noong yien-dze ’veh nung ka, ngoo tsuh-tuh ding (or li-khe noong).
Beginning with next month I promise to increase one dollar; next year I will again raise you one dollar.
下个月起頭我應許加儂一塊, 到開年我再加儂一塊

l.hi: ‘Au-kuh-nyoeh chi-deu ngoo iung-hyui ka noong ih-khwe, tau khe-nien ngoo tse ka noong ih-khwe.

div.head: THE GENTLEMEN’S TAILOR (栽縫).
div.p: [For morning coat, and such articles of apparel as are not used by the Chinese, there is no proper Chinese equivalent.]

lg.l: I want you to make a suit of clothes.

l.hi: Ngoo iau noong tsoo ih-thau i-zaung.

lg.l: Make me a pair of trousers.
Have you got your patterns with you?

l.hi: Noong siang di-kuh poo hau-yoong va?

lg.l: I want a lighter cloth for summer wear.
我要薄點个布, 爲之夏天咾用

l.hi: Ngoo iau bok-tien kuh poo, we-ts ‘au-thien lau yoong.

lg.l: 我要儂做來配身 (or 合式个)
Ngoo iau noong tsoo-le phe-sung (or ’eh-suh kuh.)
How long will it take to finish? [How much labour is there?]
When will it be ready to try on?
幾時可以拿來試試看 (or 演演看)
This overcoat is tight across the shoulders.

l.hi: Di-jien doo-i kuh kyien-paung thuh kyung.

lg.l: The vest is too loose across the chest.
The trousers must have side pockets.
I want you to mend these trousers.

l.hi: Di diau khoo-ts iau noong sieu.

lg.l: Put new cuffs on these shirts.
[This] shirt front is frayed; I want a new one.
汗衫个前面壞者, 要換新个

l.hi: ‘Oen-san kuh zien-mien wa-tse, iau wen sing-kuh.

lg.l: The material is mine, how much for making only?
料作我自辦, 不過做工要幾錢

l.hi: Liau-tsauk ngoo z-ban, peh-koo tsoo-koong iau kyi-dien?

lg.l: I want you to make a dress.
Ngoo iau noong tsoo ih-thau i-zaung.*
* This is the same expression that is used for a suit of clothes.
I want you to make a skirt.

l.hi: Ngoo iau noong tsoo ih-diau juin.

lg.l: I want you to make a bodice.

l.hi: Ngoo iau noong tsoo ih-kuh doo-teu.

lg.l: I want you to make a jacket.

l.hi: Ngoo iau noong tsoo ih-jien mo-kwo.

lg.l: I want you to make a cloak.
我要儂做一件外罩个袍褂

l.hi: Ngoo iau noong tsoo ih-jien nga-tsau-kuh bau-kwo.

lg.l: This sleeve is too long; make it shorter.
第个袖子忒長; 要做來短點

l.hi: Di-kuh zieu-ts thuh dzang; iau tsoo-le toen-tien.

lg.l: This garment is too tight; make it easier.
第件衣裳身胚忒緊,要做來寬點

l.hi: Di-jien i-zaung sung-phe thuh kyung; iau tsoo-le khwen tien.

lg.l: This is too wide (or loose); make tighter.
第件衣裳身胚忒寬, 要做來緊點

l.hi: Di-jien i-zaung sung-phe thuh khwen; iau tsoo-le kyung tien.

lg.l: Please bring me samples of native cloth (to let me see).
請儂擔點本地布个樣子撥我看看

l.hi: Tshing noong tan tien pung-di poo-kuh yang-ts, peh-ngoo khoen-khoen.

lg.l: Please bring me samples of foreign cloth (to let me see).
請儂擔點外國布个樣子撥我看看
Tshing noong tan tien nga-kok poo-kuh yang-ts, peh ngoo khoen-khoen.
Have you samples of grass cloth?
What you have of broad and narrow cloth, bring and let me see.
所有闊咾狹个布, 全擔來讓我看看

l.hi: Soo yeu khweh lau ‘ah kuh poo, zen tan-le nyang ngoo khoen-khoen.

lg.l: 幾時可以做好 (or 做得好)
I want you to do it quicker.
Can you finish it this week?
拉第个禮拜裏, 做得好否

l.hi: La di-kuh li-pa li, tsoo-tuh hau va?

lg.l: This week it is impossible to finish.
拉第个禮拜裏, 來勿及做好

l.hi: La di-kuh li-pa li, le-’veh-ji tsoo-hau.

lg.l: Then next week certainly must finish.
蓋末下个禮拜, 一定要做好
How much will it cost to make these clothes?
You ask too big a price.
Yes (or all right), I can pay you this price.
好个, 我可以撥儂第个價錢

l.hi: Hau-kuh, ngoo khau-i peh noong di-kuh ka-dieh.

lg.l: Why have you not done as I told you?
爲啥勿照我告訴儂个様子咾做

l.hi: We-sa ’veh tsau ngoo kau-soo noong-kuh yang-ts lau tsoo?

lg.l: You have done very well. When I have more work I shall want you to do it (lit., and another time I will want you to do work.)
儂做來蠻好, 下回我還要儂做
Noong tsoo-le ’man-hau; ‘au-we ngoo wan iau noong tsoo.
Take these clothes and wash them.
第个衣裳擔去淨 (or 汏)
Be careful in washing this; and do not tear it.
要當心淨; 勿要淨破
This garment wants starch, but do not make it too stiff.
第件衣裳要用點䊢, 但是勿要忒硬

l.hi: Di-jien i-zaung iau yoong tien tsiang, dan-z ’veh iau thuh ngang.

lg.l: See, you have torn this garment.
諾, 看看, 第件衣裳撥儂弄壞者

l.hi: Nau! khoen-khoen! di-jien i-zaung peh noong loong-wa-tse.

lg.l: See, this window curtain has been spoiled by you.
儂看, 第个窗帘撥儂弄壞者

l.hi: Noong khoen, di-kuh tshaung-lien peh noong loong-wa-tse.
Loong auh tshauh tse; iau tse zing.

lg.l: One piece is still missing, why?
還缺少一件, 啥緣故
It is lost; I will try to find it.
失脫者, 我再要尋尋看

l.hi: Seh-theh tse; ngoo tse iau zing-zing-khoen.

lg.l: If you cannot find it, you must pay for it.
若是尋勿著, 要儂賠个

l.hi: Zah-z zing-’veh-dzak, iau noong be kuh.

lg.l: What is the price for washing one piece?
Bring these clothes back in two or three days.
第件衣裳兩三日就要擔來

l.hi: Di-jien i-zaung liang san nyih zieu iau tan-le.

lg.l: I am going away (or leaving Shanghai) presently.
我就要出門 (or 我就要離開上海)
Ngoo zieu iau tsheh-mung (or ngoo zieu iau li-khe Zaung-he).
So you must bring back my clothes at once.
These clothes are not ironed properly; iron them again.
第件衣裳燙來勿好, 要再燙

l.hi: Di-jien i-zaung thaung-le ’veh hau; iau tse thaung.

lg.l: These clothes are not washed properly, wash them again.
第件衣裳淨來勿乾淨, 要再淨

l.hi: Di-jien i-zaung zing le ’veh koen-zing, iau tse zing.

lg.l: Don’t put any soda in the water.
As it easily takes out the colour.
How many pieces have you washed this month?
第个月裡淨之幾件衣裳
Those stirrup irons are not bright (or not clean).
馬踏櫈个鐵擦來勿亮 or 勿乾淨
Mo-dah-tung-kuh thih tshah le ’veh liang (or veh koen-zing).
Have you put on the saddle-cloth?
When did you feed the pony?

l.hi: Iau peh hau-kuh mo-liau yi chuh.

lg.l: That saddle does not fit properly.
馬鞍子裝來勿好 (or 勿妥帖)
Mo-oen-ts tsaung le ’veh hau (or veh thoo thih).

l.hi: Yien-dze ’veh iau peh sa yi chuh.

lg.l: 伊是頂熱 (or 伊是熱得極拉)
Yi z ting nyih (or Yi z nyih tuh-juh la).
Go and get the veterinary surgeon.
Hold him until I get on.
Put more straw in his stall (or box.)
The pony is very dirty; give him a good rub-down.
馬齷齪來; 要刷乾淨

l.hi: Mo auh-thsauh le; iau seh koen-zing.

lg.l: Are there candles in the lamps?
It will hurt the horse’s shoulder.
Keep the harness clean and in good order.
馬傢生要乾淨咾合式个

l.hi: Mo ka-sang iau koen-zing lau ’eh-suh kuh.

lg.l: Stay here until I come back.

l.hi: Ding la tsh-di, tung ngoo tsen-le.

lg.l: I want the carriage at nine o’clock.
伊要逃走 or 跑開

Wood Carvings.

Cloisonné ware.

Boxes of puzzles.
七巧板

A blue bowl with cover.
淡描蓋碗
Dan-miau ke-’wen.

香爐
Hyang-loo.

lg.l: 儂个貨色請儂撥我看看

l.hi: Noong-kuh hoo-suh tshing noong peh ngoo khoen-khoen.

lg.l: What is the price of this?
每塊香港洋錢齾脫幾化

How many Mexican dollars will an English sovereign bring?

l.hi: Me paung kyung-yang dzuk Iung-yang kyi-hau?

lg.l: What is the value of American dollars?

l.hi: Zak-z ’me nyih dok ih tien-tsoong iau pah-khwe yang-dien.

lg.l: What book do you think I should study?
[To teacher] Should I learn to write the characters?
儂想我要學寫中國字否

l.hi: Noong siang ngoo iau ’auh sia Tsoong-kok z va?

lg.l: [To student] You do not speak distinctly.
To listen to other people’s idiom is important.
聼別人个話法是要緊个
[We have] finished the study of this book; may [we] study Yates’ Lessons?

Di pung su dok-wen-ts, khau-i dok Tsoong-kok Yuk Nyui Miau Fah va?

Sir, please write a letter for me.
先生請儂替我寫一封信

l.hi: Sien-sang, tshing noong thi ngoo sia ih foong sing.

明朝我有事體, 勿能讀書

l.hi: Ming-tsau ngoo yeu z-thi, ’veh nung dok-su.

lg.l: [To student] The day after to-morrow I go from home and cannot come to teach.
後日我要出門, 勿能來敎書

l.hi: ‘Eu-nyih ngoo iau tsheh-mung, ’veh nung le kau su.

lg.l: At the beginning, of next week I want to go to the hills for a summer holiday, so in the meantime we will stop for a week.
下禮拜起, 我要上山歇夏, 所以暫時停一个月

l.hi: ‘Au li-pa chi, ngoo iau zaung san hyih ‘au, soo-i dzan z ding ih-kuh nyoeh.

div.p: In this and the following sections a number of useful words are grouped according to grammatical or topical divisions. A study of the words, called classifiers, which come between “a” or “an” (or rather its equivalent, the numeral 一 ih) and the word itself, will make our communications to the Chinese correct and more lucid.

list.item: Obvious typographical errors have been corrected in this text. English word hyphenation has been standardized.
Footnotes have been placed after the associated section phrase.
This book contains some rarely used forms of some Chinese characters. Any eReader should contain as full a set of fonts as possible.
Characters not found in the Unicode 13 set are replaced by ‘[Cn]’ where ‘n’ is a unique number. Images and descriptions of the unknown characters are at the end of the book.
